F1.Q1: Dressed stone slabs — cut rectangular flagging, sandy-brown, laid tight with thin joints. Not brick, not tile, not dirt. Something like a sandstone or limestone paving.
F1.Q1_WHY: The rectangles are *cut sizes*, not modules — at x460–620/y40–150 a single slab runs ~85px wide and ~28px tall, sitting beside squares of ~30×30 and a tall ~24×55. That size spread is stonecutting, not manufacture. Joints are thin dark lines, not raked mortar beds. And the cracks at x415/y16 running south, and the arc across x280–620/y300–388, propagate *across* slab boundaries and change direction without stopping — stone fails like that, wood and tile don't.
F1.Q2:
West, toward the opening at x0–188 / y145–265.

Nothing about the ground drove that. I picked it because it's a two-tile-wide opening versus a one-tile corridor south, and because it's closer. I checked the ground in front of both before answering and it is the same ground: same slab sizes, same mark density, same hue. The floor did not vote.
F1.Q3:
It has been cracked and it has been scratched, and that is the whole list. A real crack network runs through it — a main fracture entering the north wall at x≈415 and travelling south-southwest past the figure to about x355/y250, then on down to the bottom edge; a second from the west wall at (188,205) angling down-right; a branching set of arcs through the lower third. Those are good. Over the rest of it, every slab carries the same handful of scratch motifs at the same density.

What has *not* happened to it: nothing has been spilled on it, nothing has been dragged across it, nothing has been repaired, nothing has been worn. There is no dirt. For a floor in an administered underworld under four hundred years of orc garrison and however many centuries before that, it is remarkably clean.
F1.Q3_WHY: Detail density measured per 20px cell across the normalised floor sits in a band of roughly 0.08–0.18 across essentially the entire room — the only cells that fall outside are the sprite and the blank slabs listed in Q4. There is no contiguous low-detail region (polish) and no contiguous high-detail region (accumulation). Six flat dark slabs read at first glance as stains or pits, but magnified at (530,200)–(624,236) the rectangle has hard edges exactly on the slab bounds, no rim, no shadow, no falloff. It is not a stain and not a hole. It is a slab with the texture layer left off.
F1.Q4:
Two things.

**The blank slabs.** Six of them: (285,128)–(345,152), (370,120)–(414,145), (500,86)–(556,116), (455,190)–(508,216), (530,200)–(624,236), (200,290)–(276,325). They are flat value blocks with no marks at all. Because everything else on the floor is mid-frequency scratch, these read as holes in the texture and the eye snaps to them. The one at (455,190)–(508,216) sits immediately right of the figure and competes with the character sprite at 1:1.

**The "/" hatch.** A set of parallel 45° scratches running bottom-left to top-right. Once you see it you cannot stop seeing it — (470,50)–(556,80), (555,120)–(600,150), (490,240)–(540,270), (420,300)–(470,330), (240,60)–(300,110), and dozens more. It is on the majority of marked slabs, at the same angle, at the same spacing, in roughly the same quantity. It stops being scratches and becomes a screen door.
F1.Q5:
**Made** — but only just, and it's the layout doing the work, not the surface.

The slab arrangement is genuinely non-repeating. I ran autocorrelation on the flattened floor and there is no periodic peak at any lag from 1 to 60px; the correlation decays monotonically. I also block-matched at every plausible tile size (24/28/30/31/32/36px) and found no exact duplicate anywhere. Nobody stamped a tileset here.

What saves it is the crack network. Cracks are the one element that knows about the room as a whole rather than about individual slabs.

What undercuts it is the mark vocabulary. There are four motifs — the 45° hatch, rows of short horizontal dashes, vertical tally strokes of three to six, and blank. Roughly 150 slabs, four motifs, randomised offset. It isn't a repeated *image*, but it is a repeated *decision*, and at a glance those feel the same.
F1.Q6:
**YES.**

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent.** The layout is above average and the cracks are properly good. The surface is not. A floor that is genuinely good tells you something you didn't know before you looked at it; this one tells you "stone, old" and stops.
F1.Q7:
*Legible at 1:1, unmagnified:*
- The joints between slabs, and therefore the slab sizes — but that's layout, which you excluded.
- The crack network. Clearly. This is the only surface event that reads at playing size.
- The blank dark rectangles as value blocks.
- In the brightest zone only, a faint directional streaking — enough to know the surface isn't smooth, not enough to know what made the marks.

*Only appears once magnified:*
- That the streaking is 45° parallel hatch sets.
- The rows of horizontal dashes. Completely invisible at 1:1.
- The vertical tally strokes. Same.
- Individual chips and pits.
- That many slabs in the centre have *dotted* border lines rather than solid ones.

So: the faces are not blank at 1:1, but they are **generic**. You get "texture" and no information. Everything that distinguishes one slab from another required magnification, which is hunting.
F1.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1: x460–620/y40–150 (the brightest slabs, best case) — read as mottled with faint streaks, no motif identifiable. x340–470/y150–230, the halo around the figure — same. x200–300/y290–370 — read as flat brown, nothing. x250–430/y18–60 along the north wall — nothing.

Had to magnify (4× NEAREST): (440,40)–(570,110) to resolve the hatch and a chip; (510,190)–(640,250) to establish the dark rectangle had no rim; (180,180)–(340,380) to find the dashes and tallies; (185,275)–(300,340) to confirm the dark slab was blank rather than dim.

Supporting number: median floor luminance is 66/255, and **53.6% of the floor sits below luminance 70** — surface marks in that half are physically not resolvable at 1:1. Half the surface work is being spent where nobody can see it.
F1.Q8: **One age everywhere — a few centuries. Old, but not older than the records.** And that uniformity is the problem, because this place should be a palimpsest and it reads as a single pour.
F1.Q8_WHY:
The cracking at x415/y16→x355/y250 and the arcs at x280–620/y300–388 are mature — they've propagated across many slabs, which takes long settlement. That's the "centuries" read. But nothing anywhere reads *older* or *newer* than anything else: no slab is more broken than its neighbour, no section is replacement stone, no patch is fresher. I checked (200,290)–(276,325) in the south-west against (500,86)–(556,116) in the north-east — opposite corners of the room, and their mark density and mark type are indistinguishable.

Most telling: there is no repair. The fiction says a garrison has been holding and mending this place for four hundred years with rope, pins, hide and salvaged timber. Not one slab here has been lifted, replaced, shimmed, pinned or planked over. A floor under that kind of custody would be a patchwork of ages. This one has no seams of history in it at all — which, read straight, means it was laid once and abandoned, not administered.
F1.Q9:
Route: enter west at (0–188, 145–265), cross east-southeast through (250,230) → (340,260) → (400,320), then south into the corridor mouth at (377–437, 388) and out the bottom. Roughly 12 tiles.

**The ground told me nothing. I routed entirely off the walls.** That is the honest answer.
F1.Q9_WHY: Along the route — (200,220), (280,250), (350,290), (400,350) — the ground is slab, hatched, mid-brown, undifferentiated. The regions I rejected — the north strip at (250–450, 20–80), the whole east third at (500–620, 60–340) — are slab, hatched, mid-brown, undifferentiated. **The difference between the ground I walked on and the ground I rejected is zero.** Measured: normalised detail density along the route averages ~0.12; in the rejected east third it averages ~0.16, and that gap is lighting, not surface. The only spatial signal on this floor is the crack running near the route, and cracks are geology — they tell you the building settled, not where anyone walked.
F1.Q10:
**They look the same.**

In front of the west opening — x188–250, y150–265 — the slabs are the same size, the same hue, carry the same hatch, at the same density as the room's interior. In front of the south corridor mouth — x360–450, y340–388 — identical. Neither threshold is darkened, polished, chipped, dished, or scuffed. Neither has debris pushed to its sides.

A one-tile corridor south is a choke point; four hundred years of a garrison moving through it would have dished the stone in the middle of that opening and left the corners of the room untouched. Nothing distinguishes them. The floor has no opinion about its own doors.

---
F1.CULL:
Wear is uniform everywhere; four centuries of traffic recorded as evenly-scattered noise and no path.

I should add the hard version of that, because it's what causes it: across the entire lit floor, hue runs 27.9°–29.4° and saturation 0.53–0.56 at the 5th–95th percentiles. Every mark on this surface is the same colour as the slab under it, differing only in value. That isn't stone — that's a single ramp with noise on it.
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Carve a traffic lane: a band ~2 tiles wide from the west opening (188,200) through (350,280) to the south corridor mouth (400,388), rendered as *smoothed and darkened* stone — reduce mark density inside it by half and drop its value ~15%, with the untrodden corners at (500–620,60–160) and (200–280,300–380) keeping full scratch.
- Dish the south corridor mouth at (377–437, 360–400): the centre of a one-tile choke worn concave and lipped, with the walked stone visibly lower and rounder than the slabs flanking it.
- Introduce hue variation to the surface. Marks must not be the parent slab's colour darkened. Add at minimum a cool grey-green damp cast in the unlit south-west (200–300, 300–388) and a desaturated soot-grey in the crack channels — target a hue spread of at least 20°, not the current 1.5°.
- Fill or justify the six blank slabs — (285,128), (370,120), (500,86), (455,190), (530,200), (200,290). Either give them surface treatment matching their neighbours, or commit and make them actual absences: broken-out voids with a chipped rim, an interior shadow, and one salvaged timber plank pinned across the largest.
- Replace the "/" hatch monoculture. Cap any single mark motif at roughly a third of marked slabs, and add at least two motifs that read at 1:1 in the lit halo — gouges with a lifted lighter edge, and a driven pin or cramp repairing a cracked slab where the main fracture crosses (355,250).

F2.Q1: Cut stone flagging — grey-brown rectangular slabs laid in irregular courses. But I am naming that from the *layout*, not the *surface*. If you covered the joints I could not tell you whether it is stone, poured concrete, or rammed earth blocks.
F2.Q1_WHY:
The joint grid is unambiguous — slabs of varying width (16, 32, 48, 64px) in courses of varying height, e.g. the run at (460–620, 165–200) where a 32-wide, a 48-wide and a 64-wide sit in one course. That's cut masonry. What's absent is any material tell on the face: no grain, no aggregate, no bedding planes, no differential polish, no colour variation between slabs beyond a flat value shift. Slab interiors measure std 11–18 of 255 — about 7% contrast. That's mottle, not material.

---
F2.Q2:
South, into the corridor mouth at (370–437, 395).

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I chose it from the walls — the south gap is the only opening I can see *continue* off the bottom edge of the frame, so it reads as leading somewhere. The floor inside that mouth is indistinguishable from the floor at the west mouth at (185, 150–290) and indistinguishable from the floor under the figure's feet. If you swapped the two mouths I would not notice.

---
F2.Q3:
It has been cracked and pocked, and nothing else. A branching dark fracture network runs across it — one large system entering at (365, 0), descending through (330, 120), (300, 230), (270, 300) to (240, 355); a second from (450, 215) through (500, 340) to (470, 390); a third at (530, 270)→(625, 330). Scattered across it are circular ring-shaped spalls roughly 20–24px across.

Beyond that: nothing has happened. No wear. No traffic. No repair. No debris, no spill, no stain, no accumulation in corners, no chipped edges at the doorways. No rope, no pins, no timber, no hide — nothing from the orcs who are supposedly four centuries into holding this line.
F2.Q3_WHY:
I flattened the lighting and measured mean albedo in 32px blocks across the room. Interior values run 0.86–1.00 with essentially no structure — no gradient, no path, no darker zone, no lighter zone. The variation that does exist is per-slab value jitter, not spatial. The lower edge values (0.65–0.77) are normalization artefacts at the room boundary, not real. The floor at (250, 220) and the floor at (560, 120) are, statistically, the same floor.

---
F2.Q4:
Yes — the circular ring motif. A ring of pale pixels around a dark mottled centre, ~20–24px diameter. I count roughly fifteen in one screen:

(335, 42), (475, 45), (400, 100), (215, 152), (585, 190), (610, 232), (490, 290), (412, 292), (605, 305), (267, 355), (415, 375), (472, 372) — plus four more in the unlit west corridor at (30, 185), (72, 178), (35, 232), (150, 258).

They are evenly scattered — roughly one per 100px — which is what makes them read as a distribution rather than as events. I want to be precise about the nature of the repetition: I template-matched one against the rest and got correlations of only 0.30–0.33, so they are **not** pixel-identical copies. They are individually varied instances of one idea. But the idea is the same idea fifteen times, at the same scale, with no visible cause. Several of them — (335, 42), (585, 190), (610, 232) — sit nowhere near a crack. That decoupling is the tell. If they were spall from the fracture network they would cluster on it. They don't, so they read as scatter, and once I noticed that I could not stop counting them.

---
F2.Q5:
Split, and the split is the problem: **the layout was made, the surface was repeated.**

Made: I tested for global tiling and found none. Vertical autocorrelation across the floor peaks at 0.12 at a 64px shift and sits at 0.06–0.10 everywhere else — there is no repeating tile period. The slab sizes and course breaks genuinely vary.

Repeated: the *faces* draw from a vocabulary of about four marks and nothing else — 45° hatch strokes, clusters of short axis-aligned notches, blank, and the ring. You can see the whole vocabulary in one crop at (460–620, 90–200): hatched slab, notched slab, hatched slab, blank slab, notched slab. A gradient-orientation histogram over the floor gives peaks at 0°/90° (joints and notches, ~1900 each) and near-equal peaks at 45° and 135° (~1650/1590) — so the hatching does run both ways, which is better than I first suspected. But it is the same stroke weight and the same spacing in every instance. Nothing on this floor was authored for its position. Every slab could be swapped with any other slab.

---
F2.Q6:
**YES.** It is more than assembled enough to ship; the masonry variety alone puts it above a lot of what does ship.

Is it genuinely good? **No.** It is competent. The competence is real and it's in the layout — irregular ashlar with no detectable tile period is not easy and someone did it properly. But competence in the layout is doing all the work, and the surface is not holding up its end. Good would mean the ground carries information. This ground carries decoration.

---
F2.Q7:
Legible at 1:1:
- The joint grid.
- The dark branching fracture network, and the pale thread-cracks that shadow it.
- The ring motifs — these do read at 1:1, as pale smudged circles. They're the only face-level feature that survives.
- Two or three solid dark slabs that read as holes or as tonal gaps.
- Beneath all that, an undifferentiated brown mottle.

Only appears once magnified:
- The 45° hatching. At 1:1 it is dither noise.
- The notch clusters — the short bars and L-shapes that at 4× look like tool marks or illegible inscription. At 1:1 they are indistinguishable from the hatching.
- All per-slab differentiation. At 1:1 the slabs differ in value, not in character.

So: **the faces are effectively blank at 1:1.** There is detail on them — measurably, std 11–18 — but it resolves as texture-grain, not as anything a player could read. Everything that gives this floor its character at 4× is hunting, not seeing.
F2.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1: the full 750×600 view, and a native-size crop of (460–620, 90–200) viewed without scaling — in that crop I can distinguish light rectangles from dark rectangles and see two bright thread-cracks, and that is all. Also 1:1 at the south mouth, (340–470, 340–440). Had to magnify: (480–620, 60–200) at 4× to resolve the notch marks; (370–440, 70–140) at 5× to resolve the ring at (400,100) as a ring rather than a smudge; (190–330, 10–150) at 4× to find the hatching.

---
F2.Q8:
It reads as **one age everywhere** — and that uniformity is itself the finding.

Age: a few centuries. Old enough to have fractured through, not old enough to have been touched since. What it does *not* read as is a floor that has been in continuous heavy use since before the records begin, because such a floor would be a palimpsest — original slabs, replacements, replacements of replacements, patches over the patches. This is one casting.
F2.Q8_WHY:
The 32px albedo grid across the room interior returns 0.86–1.00 with no spatial structure — no zone is more worn, weathered or replaced than another. The mark vocabulary is identical in every quarter: compare (200–340, 20–160) in the far corner against (460–620, 90–200) near the right wall and (340–470, 300–395) at the south mouth — same hatch, same notches, same ring density, same joint weight. There is not one slab that is a different age from its neighbours. No slab sits proud or sunken. No joint is wider than another. No slab is a replacement.

And nowhere on this floor is there a repair. The fiction says these floors are held by a company that has been mending things with rope and driven pins and salvaged timber for four hundred years. On the ground itself I can find no pin, no plank, no lashing, no packed rubble in a gap — not at the doorways where wear concentrates, not on the fracture line at (300, 230) where it would be needed most.

---
F2.Q9:
Route, west mouth to south mouth: enter at (185, 220) → east along y≈220 through (250, 220) and (330, 230) → (400, 260) → turn south → (405, 330) → (405, 395) into the corridor mouth.

**The ground told me nothing. I routed entirely by the walls.** That is the plain answer.
F2.Q9_WHY:
Along the route — (250, 220), (330, 230), (400, 260), (405, 330) — flattened albedo runs 0.90, 0.94, 0.96, 0.93. Regions I rejected as off-route — (560, 120), (230, 330), (600, 250) — run 0.95, 0.89, 0.92. There is no difference between the ground I would walk on and the ground I would not. Nothing is smoother, darker, more polished, more scuffed, more swept.

The one large-scale feature that could have guided me actively works against the route: the main fracture running (365, 0) → (240, 355) is the strongest directional line on the floor, and it cuts diagonally *across* my path. It's the only thing on this ground with any sense of direction to it, and it points the wrong way — because it's damage, not a way through.

---
F2.Q10:
**They all look the same.** I cannot tell.

Two openings. West mouth, ground at (185, 150–290): standard slabs, one hatched, one notched, a ring at (150, 258) just inside, albedo 0.88–0.93. South mouth, ground at (370–437, 380–400): standard slabs, notch marks, albedo 0.90–0.93, and the texture carries straight through the threshold into the corridor without a single change — no sill, no darkening, no smoothing, no scatter of grit either side.

If one of these is the door the orc company has walked through twice a day for four hundred years and the other has not been opened in living memory, the floor does not say which.

---
F2.CULL: Ground is uniform everywhere — no wear, no traffic, no repair. Reads as decorated tile, not four centuries of use.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Cut the ring motif to two or three instances per screen and place each one where something caused it — on the fracture line at (300, 230), at a doorway threshold — instead of scattering fifteen at even spacing.
- Darken and smooth a traffic lane from the west mouth (185, 220) through to the south mouth (405, 395): drop albedo ~15% and suppress face marks along it, so the route is legible before the walls are.
- Differentiate the two thresholds. Wear, polish and grit-scatter at (370–437, 385–400); intact sharp-edged slabs and accumulated debris at (185, 150–290) — or the reverse. Make one door obviously the used one.
- Put orc repair on the ground: driven pins and lashed timber across the fracture at (300, 230) and (480, 300), packed rubble in the gap, at least two slabs that are visibly later replacements sitting proud of their neighbours.
- Raise face contrast so something reads at 1:1. Slab-interior std is 11–18 of 255 and resolves as noise — either push the notch marks to roughly double that amplitude so they read as worked stone at phone size, or drop them and let the faces be honestly bare.
